tldr: Without building elevation maps or prior maps, this quadruped locomotion framework feeds raw voxelized point clouds from four LiDARs directly into a reinforcement learning policy, allowing a single policy to traverse diverse challenging terrains including steel-grating stairs, stepping stones, 80-cm gaps, and 80-cm high platforms.
hero_caption: Real-robot experiments with the quadruped robot X30 traversing various challenging terrains using a single policy. It tackles stepping stones, an 80-cm gap, an 0.8-m platform, a balance beam, climbing with a 50-kg payload, and a 2.5-km mountain route—all without maps, directly processing point clouds.
overview:
When deploying quadruped robots for plant inspection and rough-terrain exploration, recognizing and traversing terrains with discontinuous footholds—such as grating stairs, stepping stones, deep gaps, and high platforms—poses a major challenge. The prevailing conventional approach builds elevation maps from LiDARs or depth cameras, or converts sensory data into latent representations such as world models before passing them to the policy. However, elevation maps become distorted due to odometry drift and cannot properly handle see-through gratings. Depth cameras suffer from backlighting or low light, and limited fields of view leave blind spots right under the feet.

To address this, the authors propose PointWalker, which completely removes intermediate map representations and feeds raw voxelized point clouds (350 points) from four LiDAR sensors directly into a reinforcement learning policy. Geometric relationships among points are tokenized with computationally lightweight Linear Self-Attention, and a Cross-Attention mechanism—queried by proprioception (joint angles, angular velocities, etc.) and command velocities—dynamically extracts the terrain features needed for the current motion. In addition, they introduce a dual-channel simulation that faithfully reproduces the openings and treads of gratings, along with dynamic terrain-aware rewards that encourage jumping.

Using a single proximal policy optimization (PPO) run across seven extreme terrain classes in simulation, the policy is transferred zero-shot to a real Deep Robotics X30 robot. The results demonstrate that, without maps or foothold estimation, the single policy achieves jumping across an 0.8-m gap, climbing an 0.8-m platform, ascending 45-degree steel-grating stairs, carrying a 50-kg payload (91% of its body weight), and completing a 2.5-km mountain route.
contributions: Built the first mapless quadruped locomotion framework that links raw LiDAR point clouds directly to motor control without elevation maps or latent space representations.
Combined Linear Self-Attention and Cross-Attention to achieve accurate foothold perception with an onboard compute budget of just 2.01 ms (10% of the 20-ms control cycle).

Enabled a single policy to learn across seven challenging terrain classes—from grating stairs to stepping stones—using a dual-channel simulation that separates geometry from physical collision along with terrain-adaptive rewards.

Demonstrated zero-shot transfer on a real Deep Robotics X30, crossing an 0.8-m gap, climbing an 0.8-m platform, tackling 45-degree grating stairs, carrying a 50-kg payload, and finishing a 2.5-km mountain trail.

sections.heading: Why ditch elevation maps and read raw point clouds directly?
sections.summary: When quadrupeds encounter challenging terrains like gratings and stepping stones in real environments, vision that spots safe footholds before contact is indispensable. Yet conventional elevation maps and depth images face representational limits such as drift, blind spots, and failure on mesh structures. This paper proposes PointWalker, a single policy that directly consumes raw LiDAR point clouds without any intermediate map.
sections.details:
In recent years, quadruped robots have been rapidly applied to plant inspections, cargo transport, and outdoor exploration. However, these environments contain not only steep slopes and stairs, but also see-through steel gratings, wide gaps, stepping stones, and balance beams—terrains where robots will immediately fall unless they accurately capture foothold geometry before making contact.

While reinforcement learning has driven huge progress in locomotion, blind walking that relies purely on foot contact cannot handle gaps or narrow footholds. Conventional approaches have therefore used elevation maps or depth camera images. But there is a major catch: odometry drift distorts the map, outliers corrupt it, and fundamentally, 2.5D single-height maps cannot represent structures like gratings where light passes through yet feet can stand. Furthermore, depth cameras degrade in the dark or under direct sunlight, and their narrow forward cone leaves blind spots right under the robot.

LiDAR provides direct 3D geometry regardless of ambient light, but it has historically only been used to build maps or feed world models for robot control. The starting point of this research is: why not read raw point clouds directly and drive the locomotion policy? PointWalker introduces an innovative approach that takes omnidirectional raw point clouds from four LiDARs directly, traversing seven types of challenging terrains without map generation or foothold planning.

sections.heading: Evolution and limits of perceptual interfaces for legged robots
sections.summary: RL-based locomotion has evolved from proprioception-only blind control to privileged distillation, and then to visual and LiDAR integration. However, prior methods all relied on intermediate representations such as elevation maps or latent world models, making the interface itself a bottleneck for traversability. PointWalker breaks through this constraint via direct attention over raw point clouds.
sections.details:
### II-A Reinforcement Learning-based Legged Locomotion
With massively parallel simulation, RL-based quadruped locomotion has reached practical viability. A common approach trains a teacher with privileged terrain information (such as height maps) in the simulator and distills it into a student policy running solely on the robot's own proprioception. However, for stepping stones or deep gaps where robots inevitably stumble unless they look before stepping, distilling down to proprioception fundamentally lacks the necessary information and hits a wall.

### II-B Perceptual Interfaces for Agile Locomotion
This motivated active research into integrating visual information directly into policies, such as optimizing footholds using local 2.5D elevation maps or learning parkour maneuvers by convolving depth camera images directly. Yet these were still constrained by interface limitations: blind spots of forward-facing cameras (unable to see directly below or to the sides) and the update overhead and distortion of intermediate maps.

### II-C LiDAR-based Locomotion
Even with LiDAR, typical pipelines aggregate scans into elevation maps or project them onto spherical depth images for world models, interposing some intermediate representation. Raw point cloud inputs were confined to obstacle avoidance. PointWalker revamps this by directly fusing sparse, voxelized raw LiDAR points with the robot's motion history via Cross-Attention, completely eliminating the overhead and information loss of intermediate representations.

sections.heading: How to process raw points and move: The PointWalker framework
sections.summary: 350 voxel points from four LiDARs are encoded with Linear Self-Attention, and Cross-Attention queried by motion history extracts the necessary foothold features. A dual-channel simulation that reproduces gratings and terrain-adaptive rewards for jumping gaps and platforms enable highly dynamic locomotion learned in a single PPO run.
sections.details:
### III-A Onboard LiDAR Perception Pipeline
The robot mounts four Livox Mid-360 LiDARs distributed across front, rear, left, and right, covering a full 360-degree horizontal and -7 to 52-degree vertical field of view. At a 50-Hz control frequency, a total of 350 points ($5 \times 70 \times 3$ dimensions) sampled via voxelization (0.1-m grid) from the 5 most recent scan groups serve as policy input.
To process these points directly, the framework adopts Linear Self-Attention whose computational cost scales linearly with the number of points. Avoiding the quadratic cost of standard Softmax attention, it encodes point-to-point geometric structures (such as grating bar patterns) into 32-dimensional tokens with an ultralow latency of just 2.01 ms.

### III-B Cross-Attention Fusion and Policy Network
In the policy backbone, Multi-Head Cross-Attention is applied over the point cloud tokens using a feature vector $\boldsymbol{s}_t$ generated from proprioceptive history (joint angles, angular velocities, gravity vector, etc.) and target velocity commands as the query. This focuses attention specifically on the terrain points essential to current locomotion—such as the area around the next stepping foot or the opposite bank of a gap—extracting a 512-dimensional terrain context $\boldsymbol{z}_t$. Furthermore, multi-task learning with auxiliary heads predicting the robot's linear velocity and foot clearance improves the quality of the latent representations.

### III-C Terrain-Aware Reward Design
Rewards designed only for flat ground cause the robot to freeze before gaps or high platforms. This method introduces two dynamic incentives:
- **Gap Acceleration Incentive**: When detecting a gap ahead, it temporarily raises the forward target velocity to encourage a run-up and relaxes excessive-speed penalties.
- **Platform Jump Incentive**: Before a high step, it grants a reward proportional to the product of vertical velocity $v_z$ and step height, promoting a jumping maneuver that plants the front feet while thrusting strongly off the rear legs.
A "foot-edge penalty," which casts virtual rays around each foot to penalize landing near edges, encourages stable foot placement that avoids slipping off the edges of stepping stones or stairs.

### III-D Dual-Channel Simulation and Single-Stage Training
Inside the simulator, the physical collision channel and the visual perception channel are separated. On grating stairs, physics treats them as flat footholds for contact calculations, while LiDAR raycasts hit a grid mesh with 5-mm thickness and 40-mm pitch, faithfully modeling the real-world property where light passes through but feet find purchase. As a result, a single training run of Asymmetric PPO—providing privileged information only to the Critic without teacher-student distillation—yields a single policy covering all seven terrains.

captions.F2: Overall framework of PointWalker. (a) Inputs are point clouds from four LiDARs, proprioception, and velocity commands; privileged information enters only the Critic during training. (b) Points are encoded with Linear Self-Attention and fused with robot states as queries via Cross-Attention. (c) Single-policy inference runs at 50 Hz onboard an RK3588 processor.

sections.heading: Simulation evaluation and real-robot zero-shot validation
sections.summary: In simulation across seven challenging terrains, PointWalker achieved an average success rate of 90.1%, consistently outperforming elevation-map and depth-image baselines. In zero-shot transfer experiments on a real Deep Robotics X30, the single policy crossed an 80-cm gap, scaled an 80-cm platform, climbed 45-degree grating stairs, carried a 50-kg payload, and completed a 2.5-km mountain route with ease.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup and Compute Cost
The experiments used a 55-kg class Deep Robotics X30 quadruped robot. Running ONNX Runtime on the onboard embedded CPU (Rockchip RK3588), the full pipeline from point cloud voxelization to policy inference took just 2.01 ms. This is roughly 10% of the 20-ms control cycle, leaving ample compute headroom for control.

### IV-B Simulation Results and Ablations
Traversability success rates were evaluated across seven terrains in the most difficult curriculum environment:
- **Success Rates**: PointWalker achieved an average of 90.1%. In contrast, the elevation map (Height-map) baseline aggregated erroneous heights on grating stairs (86.7%) and dropped to 75.8% on stepping stones. The depth image baseline suffered heavily from blind spots beneath the robot on gaps (71.5%) and stepping stones (68.4%), averaging 84.8%. The blind policy degraded to under 30% on gaps and high platforms.
- **Module Ablations**: Replacing Cross-Attention with simple average pooling dropped the success rate by 10 points to 80.1%. Because critical foothold points make up only a fraction of the total, query-based selective extraction is essential. Coarsening the voxel size to 0.2 m prevented resolving thin beams and stair gratings, reducing the success rate to 82.2%.

### IV-C Real-Robot Experiments: Harsh Real-World Validation
The trained policy was flashed directly onto the physical X30 and tested without any fine-tuning:
- **Traversing Extreme Terrains**: It smoothly climbed 45-degree steel-grating stairs (25-cm step height). Attention visualizations show focus sharply concentrated only on the currently supporting tread and the next target tread. It also bounded over an 80-cm wide gap, climbed an 80-cm high platform by hooking its front legs, and traversed a 35-cm wide balance beam and stepping stones with precision.
- **Robustness and Heavy Loads**: Even when two of the four LiDARs (front and rear) were intentionally taped over, the robot continued walking stably on stairs and slopes thanks to field-of-view redundancy and training noise injection. Furthermore, it climbed grating stairs carrying 50 kg on its back (91% of its weight), and completed a 2.5-km mountain trail with a 200-m elevation change (rocks, fallen leaves, irregular stone stairs) carrying 25 kg in 46 minutes without trouble.

sections.heading: The future of robot locomotion beyond mapping
sections.summary: By directly using raw LiDAR point clouds, PointWalker sheds the distortions and computational burden of intermediate maps, proving unprecedented versatility in rough terrain traversal. While coordinating with global navigation and tracking moving footholds remain future work due to reliance on local instantaneous perception, it establishes a powerful new standard for legged robot perception-control interfaces.
sections.details:
The most striking takeaway of this work is that neither detailed elevation maps nor foothold planners are required to traverse challenging terrains with sparse footholds. Picking up features directly from raw point clouds simultaneously resolves the fundamental issues of 2.5D maps—such as height misestimation on gratings—and depth cameras—such as foot blind spots caused by field-of-view constraints.

On the other hand, the current implementation operates solely on local, instantaneous point clouds around the robot. To bypass global obstacles outside the field of view or determine optimal paths to a destination, integration with a higher-level global path planning layer (Navigation Stack) is required. Additionally, the setup is tailored to four LiDARs; evaluating transferability to other platforms with different sensor configurations, as well as tracking wobbly suspension bridges or moving footholds, presents compelling future research directions.

takeaways: Connecting raw point clouds directly to control—bypassing intermediate representations like elevation maps or world models—avoids geometric failure on unique terrains such as gratings and stepping stones.
Combining low-complexity Linear Self-Attention with motion-state-queried Cross-Attention enables ultra-fast point cloud processing and control in 2.01 ms on an embedded CPU.
A dual-channel simulation that separates geometric perception (LiDAR) from physical collision closes the sim-to-real gap for real-world see-through materials.
Explicit terrain-adaptive reward incentives are highly effective for aggressive dynamic maneuvers like gap run-ups and platform leaps that standard velocity-tracking rewards tend to penalize.
limitations: Point cloud processing is currently limited to a local observation window of the past 0.1 seconds, lacking the ability to avoid obstacles several meters away and select global routes.
The approach assumes a specific hardware setup with four LiDARs at the robot's corners; generalizability to platforms with fewer sensors or different placements remains unverified.
Adapting to dynamically shifting or deformable supports over time, such as collapsing rubble or swaying footholds, remains an open challenge.
